originalTitle: What Is The Biggest Threat To Constellation Brands Stock?

content:

Constellation Brands (STZ) shareholders have lagged behind the broader market. The stock lost 2.7%, dividends included, over the year to October 20, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned 17.1%. Management said on the October 7 call that the latest quarter beat its own expectations. Yet the company also hinted at a pressure that could outlast one good quarter. So what is that pressure, and who is raising it?

Constellation Brands Is Holding Back On Prices

Management said on the fiscal Q2 2027 call that it intended to land at the lower end of its long-run pricing range of 1% to 2% in fiscal 2027, because the company has kept price increases selective given the macroeconomic backdrop. Pricing net of mix was roughly flat during the quarter. Management pointed to mix headwinds, along with distributor incentives and couponing used to support demand, to explain why pricing net of mix was flat.

Flat pricing stings more when costs rise. An analyst on the same call asked whether inflation in the back half of the year would weigh on gross margins. Management pushed back. The company said that the second half brings its lowest volume period of the year and less fixed cost absorption, calling the pattern normal seasonality.

A known cost is also on the way. Management expects to place its Veracruz site in service at the beginning of fiscal 2028, adding about $75 million of depreciation a year. Management estimated this at about 90 basis points of margin headwind. That spells out the threat in plain terms: prices that barely rise while a known new cost arrives in fiscal 2028.

How Much Of Constellation Brands’ Sales Come From Beer?

About 91% of them. Beer brought in $8.32 billion of Constellation Brands’ $9.14 billion of revenue in fiscal 2026, which ended February 28, 2026. Beer revenue fell 2.6% that year after rising 4.6% in fiscal 2025. This means the business most exposed to flat prices was already shrinking.

Investors already pay little for a stock whose main business shrank last fiscal year. The shares trade at 11.8 times trailing earnings, compared against 23.0 for the S&P 500. They were priced at 2.1 times sales at the August 31, 2026 quarter end, marking the lowest of the 40 quarter ends in our data, which starts at fiscal Q3 2017. They fetched 6.0 times sales at the end of 2017, the highest in that span. The latest close was also 19.2% below the stock’s highest close of the past year, reached on February 4, 2026. The price appears to assume little growth from here.

How Worried Should Constellation Brands Holders Be?

The squeeze is real, but it builds slowly. Management said the company is hedged at or above 90% for most commodities and currencies in fiscal 2027, and fully hedged on diesel. Management also said it has begun layering in hedges for fiscal 2028 and beyond. Management reiterated its fiscal 2027 guidance for comparable earnings per share of $11.20 to $11.90, a forecast rather than a result. That makes flat pricing a risk to watch rather than an immediate worry, though the Veracruz cost begins in March 2027.

Pricing net of mix is the measure to watch when Constellation Brands next reports, expected on or around January 5, 2027.

Does This Mean You Should Act On STZ?

Our purpose is to inform you with unique data so you can make the right investment decisions. That said, betting on a single stock is always risky, no matter which direction you choose.

There is a smarter approach. Since its inception, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has returned 105%, beating the benchmark that combines the three major indices – the S&P 500, S&P Mid-cap, and Russell 2000. And it did so without taking the concentrated risk that comes with do-it-yourself stock picking. If that is how you want to invest, the HQ Portfolio is the place to start.
